props.gloss_en: the mishnah's principle: whatever is susceptible to impurity or does not grow from the ground may not be used as sekhakh
Reish Lakish: the sekhakh law derives from 'and a mist went up from the earth' -- as mist, so sekhakh
the stam: the mist-derivation works for the one who says the desert sukkot were clouds of glory -- R' Eliezer
the stam's question: for R' Akiva, who says they made actual sukkot, what source can be given?
R' Eliezer: the sukkot of 'I made the children of Israel dwell in sukkot' (Vayikra 23:43) were clouds of glory
R' Akiva: they made themselves actual sukkot

R' Yochanan per Rav Dimi: 'the festival of sukkot you shall make for yourself' (Devarim 16:13) juxtaposes sukkah to the festival-offering; as the chagiga is not susceptible to impurity and grows from the ground, so the sukkah
R' Yochanan per Ravin: the sekhakh law derives from 'when you gather in from your threshing floor and from your winepress' (Devarim 16:13)
...the verse speaks of the waste of the threshing floor and the winepress (Steinsaltz: stalks and vines)
R' Zeira: 'winepress' is written, and one cannot roof with it -- so the verse cannot mean the winepress itself
Rav Ashi: 'FROM your threshing floor' -- not the threshing floor itself; 'FROM your winepress' -- not the winepress itself
Rav Chisda: the sekhakh law derives from 'go out to the mountain and bring olive leaves, and oil-tree leaves, and myrtle leaves, and palm leaves, and leaves of a thick tree' (Nechemya 8:15)
Rav Chisda: the verse's 'myrtle' is wild myrtle, for the sukkah
Rav Chisda: and the 'thick tree' is for the lulav
